title: Domestic Flights Carry New Risks for Visa Holders as ICE Expands Airport Enforcement
excerpt: TSA is sharing passenger data with ICE, leading to immigration arrests at 15 or more major airports. Even travelers with valid work permits and pending cases have faced detention.
body:
• The Transportation Security Administration is now sharing domestic passenger manifest data with ICE, which cross-references it against immigration databases to identify and detain travelers.
  • Immigration arrests have been confirmed at 15 or more major US airports, including LAX, SFO, Philadelphia, and Reagan National, affecting people with visa overstays, pending cases, and even valid work permits.
  • The American Immigration Lawyers Association advises all non-citizens to verify their I-94 status at i94.cbp.dhs.gov and carry their passport, I-94 printout, and I-797 approval notice when flying domestically.
  • Since May 2025, only REAL ID-compliant licenses, foreign passports, green cards, and employment authorization documents are accepted at TSA checkpoints for domestic flights.

Airports Emerge as Immigration Enforcement Front Line

Domestic air travel in the United States has entered a new era for non-citizens. A policy shift that began quietly in early 2025 has turned airports into active immigration enforcement zones, with the Transportation Security Administration now sharing passenger data with Immigration and Customs Enforcement on a routine basis.

https://x.com/Gianl1974/status/2096659046820651185

ICE confirmed in late July 2026 that TSA provides passenger manifest information — names, dates of birth, and flight details — that is cross-referenced against immigration databases. When matches are found, ICE dispatches agents to airports to detain individuals before boarding or at domestic gates.

The Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA) and the American Immigration Lawyers Association issued a joint warning on August 2, 2026, after a sharp rise in airport detentions. Immigration arrests have been confirmed at 15 or more major airports, including Los Angeles (LAX), San Francisco (SFO), Philadelphia (PHL), Reagan National (DCA), Dulles (IAD), and Baltimore-Washington (BWI), with additional incidents reported across Nevada, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Texas, and Virginia.

Who Is Being Detained

The enforcement sweep extends well beyond people with criminal records or active deportation orders. According to the CHIRLA advisory, airport operations now target visa overstays with no criminal record, applicants with pending adjustment-of-status cases or asylum claims, and people carrying valid work permits or Advance Parole documents.

Attorneys report that travelers with Advance Parole — documents specifically designed to permit travel — have been held for hours at airports. In some cases, officials questioned documents as part of “administrative fraud” investigations directed by DHS General Counsel James Percival since May 2026.

“This administration works diligently to ensure that foreigners who are in our country illegally can no longer fly, unless it is to leave the country and self-deport.”

— Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, August 1, 2026

In one documented case, a college student preparing to board a domestic flight from Boston for the holidays was handcuffed by ICE officers at the TSA checkpoint. The student had a prior deportation order from 2015 she did not know about. She was taken into custody and ultimately deported.

REAL ID Changes the Equation

The enforcement expansion coincides with the REAL ID Act going into full effect on May 7, 2025. All travelers 18 and older must now present a REAL ID-compliant license or other acceptable identification to board a domestic flight. State-issued driver’s licenses that are not REAL ID-compliant — including those issued to undocumented individuals in California and other states — are no longer accepted at TSA checkpoints.

Accepted identification for domestic flights now includes valid foreign passports, permanent resident cards (green cards), Employment Authorization Documents (I-766), US passports, and DHS trusted traveler cards such as Global Entry and NEXUS. Standard driver’s licenses marked “Federal Limits Apply” and the CBP One app are no longer valid for air travel.

What Non-Citizens Should Know Before Flying

The AILA advises all non-citizens to take several precautions before domestic air travel. The most critical step is checking I-94 status at i94.cbp.dhs.gov. The I-94 arrival record — not the visa stamp in a passport — controls how long a person is authorized to stay in the United States. An expired I-94 can result from changing employers without an approved H-1B transfer, dropping below full-time enrollment as an F-1 student, or working outside approved job duties.

When flying, the AILA recommends carrying a valid passport, I-94 printout, and I-797 approval notice. F-1 and J-1 students should also carry Form I-20 or DS-2019. Digital and physical copies of all documents should be maintained in case originals are confiscated.

Travelers have the right to remain silent if questioned about immigration status, the right to request an attorney, and the right to opt out of facial recognition scans at TSA checkpoints. However, exercising these rights does not prevent detention if ICE has independent legal authority based on a prior removal order or other enforcement priority.

Impact on the Diaspora Community

For Indian professionals on H-1B visas, the new enforcement reality adds another layer of complexity to life in the United States. While H-1B holders with current status face relatively low risk, the AILA warns that even routine changes — a job switch without a timely transfer petition, a brief gap in status — can create unexpected vulnerability at airports.

DHS is also consolidating biometric databases from TSA, ICE, CBP, and USCIS, including facial recognition data, into a single unified platform. TSA expanded facial recognition to 65 airports in early 2026. Travelers currently have the right to opt out of facial recognition scans during domestic flights by requesting manual ID verification.

Rights groups advise non-citizens without permanent residency to weigh the risks of air travel against alternatives. Ground transportation carries fewer enforcement touchpoints, though Border Patrol has been reported conducting document checks on long-distance buses and trains in some regions. Those with any unresolved immigration issues should consult an attorney before booking any travel.
nri_angle: Indian professionals on H-1B visas must verify their I-94 status and carry complete immigration documents for domestic flights as ICE expands airport enforcement operations.
